keyPoints: History is interpretation, not just dates — link every historical fact to its cultural meaning.
For 'history and culture' questions, always connect past events to present identity.
Love in literature is shown through action and sacrifice, not just words — cite a scene.
Life-and-love answers score best with one personal reflection plus one textual example.
Health questions test both vocabulary (diet, fitness, well-being) and argument — give reasons.
Remember: exercise benefits body AND mind; mention both for full marks.
Core tension: development vs environment — answers should weigh both sides before concluding.
Use cause–effect chains (deforestation → flood → displacement) to show reasoning.
Humour entertains; satire criticises — identify the target of the joke in exam answers.
Quote the funny line, then explain what serious point it makes.
Know the difference: democracy is a system, human rights are entitlements — define both.
Support answers with one concrete example (election, protest, law) not just theory.
Family conflict questions need both sides' perspectives before judgement.
Link theme (love, duty, generation gap) to a specific character's behaviour.
Art reflects society — connect any artwork discussed to its social context.
Use sensory vocabulary (vivid, expressive, evocative) when describing art.
Fantasy is not escape only — it mirrors real fears and desires symbolically.
Identify the 'impossible' element and explain its realistic meaning.
Career answers should include skills, planning and risk — not just ambition.
Entrepreneurship = spotting a problem and solving it profitably; state this formula.
Distinguish power (capacity) from authority (legitimate right) in definitions.
Analyse how texts show power misuse — through a character's decision, not description.
War literature focuses on human cost, not strategy — emphasise suffering and loss.
Peace answers should propose concrete steps, not just wish for harmony.
Critical thinking = questioning evidence, not rejecting everything — show balanced reasoning.
Structure: claim → evidence → evaluation → conclusion; examiners reward this order.
Globalization brings both opportunity and cultural loss — mention both effects.
Diaspora themes: identity, nostalgia, belonging; use these three keywords.
Theme: divine justice vs human justice — Aksionov suffers for a crime he did not commit.
The title's meaning: God sees the truth but waits 26 years; forgiveness ends the story.
The entire story is a child's imagination — the carpet game symbolises risk and fear.
Note the open ending: we never learn if he crosses safely; discuss why Dahl chose this.
Jonathan's optimism after war — 'Nothing puzzles God!' is the story's key line.
Theme: resilience; the theft scene shows acceptance rather than despair.
Two orphans find family feeling in each other — irony when a woman divides them.
Maupassant's twist ending: the 'third little soldier' is the baby; explain the irony.
The astrologer once left the man for dead — his guess is actually knowledge, not magic.
Irony: he earns a living by 'reading stars' but cannot read his own past; guilt resolved at dusk.
The virus speaks — personification lets corona accuse humans of destroying nature.
Central message: the pandemic was nature's warning; humans must change, not just survive.
Similes drive the poem: love compared to a red rose and a sweet melody.
Theme: eternal love — 'till a' the seas gang dry' uses hyperbole for devotion.
Extended metaphor: life as theatre; the seven ages are seven acts.
Know the stages in order — infant, schoolboy, lover, soldier, justice, pantaloon, second childhood.
The speaker addresses a small child (himself) — innocence vs adult compromise.
Unusual typography and lowercase style are part of the meaning; mention modernist technique.
Dialogue with a dead soldier-husband — irony in 'gifts': medals for a life.
Anti-war theme: war's gifts are worthless against human loss; point out the reversal.
Tradition survives only when shared — storytelling is the method of preservation.
LaPena blends Native American worldview: art, ritual and nature are one.
Three stories: dots (trust the future), love (do what you love), death (live each day fully).
'Stay hungry, stay foolish' — memorise this closing for theme questions.
A scientist's demands: work, freedom and companionship — list them explicitly.
Haldane values rational living; connect his demands to wartime context.
Poverty defined through lived detail — smell, exhaustion, humiliation, not statistics.
Note the angry, defensive tone; she refuses pity and demands understanding.
Research is humankind's survival tool — curiosity now prevents catastrophe later.
Argument structure: small findings accumulate into civilisational protection.
Women find the evidence men dismiss as 'trifles' — gender irony is the core.
The dead canary = motive; discuss the moral choice the women make.
Former lovers meet as old strangers — neither recognises the other at first.
Humour comes from vanity: both invent glamorous versions of their past.
Satire on education: Wasserkopf demands his tuition back because he learned nothing.
The teachers 'win' by out-examining him — clever twist saves the money.
